reference.source: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
clinicalPearls: Presents in older adults with oropharyngeal dysphagia, regurgitation of undigested food, halitosis, a gurgling neck and sometimes a palpable neck swelling
Regurgitation of retained food, especially at night, predisposes to cough and aspiration pneumonia
It is a false (pulsion) diverticulum, a mucosal herniation through Killian's dehiscence, a weak area between the two parts of the inferior pharyngeal constrictor
Underlying incoordination and impaired relaxation of the upper oesophageal sphincter (cricopharyngeus) drives pouch formation
Barium swallow is the preferred diagnostic test and clearly outlines the posterior midline pouch above the sphincter
Passing an endoscope or nasogastric tube blindly risks perforating the pouch, so caution is required
Symptomatic pouches are treated by dividing the cricopharyngeus with endoscopic stapling or laser, or by open surgical diverticulectomy with myotomy
reference.pathophysiology: Zenker diverticulum is an acquired outpouching of pharyngeal mucosa through Killian's dehiscence, a triangular zone of muscular weakness between the oblique and horizontal fibres of the inferior pharyngeal constrictor just above the upper oesophageal sphincter. Impaired relaxation and reduced compliance of the cricopharyngeus muscle raise hypopharyngeal pressure during swallowing, and this repeated pressure forces the mucosa and submucosa through the weak point, creating a false (pulsion) diverticulum. As the pouch enlarges it retains food and secretions, causing regurgitation, halitosis and a risk of aspiration.
additionalDifferentials: Achalasia and other oesophageal motility disorders
Peptic or other benign oesophageal stricture
Neurological causes of oropharyngeal dysphagia such as stroke or Parkinson disease
additionalInvestigations: Barium swallow to demonstrate and size the pouch
Careful upper endoscopy where malignancy needs exclusion, with awareness of perforation risk
Videofluoroscopic swallow study to assess swallowing mechanics
Assessment for aspiration including chest imaging when respiratory symptoms are present
Oesophageal manometry in selected cases to characterise sphincter dysfunction
redFlags: Significant weight loss or rapidly progressive dysphagia raising concern for malignancy
A new hard neck mass or bleeding, since carcinoma can rarely arise within a long-standing pouch
Complete dysphagia or inability to maintain nutrition and hydration
reference.prognosis: Small asymptomatic pouches may be observed, while symptomatic pouches respond well to endoscopic or surgical treatment, though recurrence and, rarely, malignant change within a chronic pouch can occur.
pitfalls: Blindly intubating the oesophagus or passing tubes and perforating the pouch
Attributing dysphagia to age or reflux without imaging the pharynx
Overlooking aspiration as a cause of recurrent chest infection
Failing to divide the cricopharyngeus, which risks recurrence after simple pouch removal
references: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
Cummings Otolaryngology - Head and Neck Surgery
management: Treat symptomatic pouches by dividing the cricopharyngeus, using endoscopic rigid stapling or flexible septotomy (including per-oral endoscopic myotomy) or open cricopharyngeal myotomy with diverticulectomy, diverticulopexy or inversion
Observe small, asymptomatic pouches with dietary and postural measures
Address the underlying upper-oesophageal-sphincter dysfunction, since cricopharyngeal myotomy is key to relieving symptoms and preventing recurrence
Reduce aspiration risk with eating advice, and treat aspiration pneumonia when it occurs
Exercise caution with blind passage of endoscopes or nasogastric tubes because of the perforation risk
Monitor for recurrence and, rarely, malignant change within a long-standing pouch
Refer to ENT or upper-gastrointestinal surgical services for definitive treatment and manage postoperative complications such as leak or fistula
